questions.question: 1. Which one of the following steps is incorrect when performing iterative DFS using a stack?

answers.a: STEP 1: Start by putting any one of the graph's vertices on top of a stack; this acts as the source vertex of DFS.
answers.b: STEP 2: Take the top item of the stack and mark it as visited.
answers.c: STEP 3: Create a list of that vertex's adjacent vertices and add the ones that have already been visited to the top of the stack.
answers.d: STEP 4: Keep repeating the process until the stack is empty.

explanations.a: Incorrect. This is a valid initialization step for an iterative DFS traversal.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Marking a vertex as visited when it is processed is part of maintaining DFS traversal state.
explanations.c: Correct. Adding already visited vertices back to the stack can cause unnecessary repeated processing; DFS should use unvisited adjacent vertices for further exploration.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Continuing until the stack becomes empty is a standard termination condition for iterative DFS.

questions.question: 2. What is the time complexity of DFS when $V$ is the number of vertices and $E$ is the number of edges, using an adjacency-list representation?

explanations.a: Incorrect. With an adjacency-list representation, DFS does not need to examine every possible pair of vertices.
explanations.b: Correct. DFS visits vertices and examines edges represented in the adjacency lists, resulting in $O(V + E)$ time.
explanations.c: Incorrect. DFS does not generally perform a quadratic operation over the edges.
explanations.d: Incorrect. DFS does not generally involve a sorting or balanced-search operation that produces $O(V \log V)$ time.

answers.b: DFS goes deeper along a path before backtracking when necessary.
answers.c: BFS explores neighbors level by level before proceeding to vertices at greater depth.
answers.d: DFS uses a queue as its defining traversal structure.

explanations.a: Incorrect. The relative memory usage of BFS and DFS can depend on the structure of the graph, so this statement is not inherently incorrect.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Exploring deeply before backtracking is the defining behavior of DFS.
explanations.c: Incorrect. BFS explores vertices level by level, processing nearer vertices before those farther from the source.
explanations.d: Correct. The standard iterative DFS uses a stack, while a queue is associated with the standard BFS implementation.

questions.question: 4. Which of the following are applications of DFS?

explanations.a: Incorrect. DFS can be used as part of topological sorting, but this option describes only one application.
explanations.b: Incorrect. DFS can be used to detect cycles, but this option describes only one application.
explanations.c: Incorrect. DFS can be used to find connected components, but this option describes only one application.
explanations.d: Correct. DFS is commonly used for topological sorting, cycle detection, and finding connected components.

questions.question: 5. DFS can only be applied to trees and not to graphs.

explanations.a: Incorrect. DFS is a graph traversal technique and can be applied to general graphs as well as trees.
explanations.b: Correct. A tree is a special type of graph, and DFS can be applied to both trees and general graphs.

answers.a: DFS uses exhaustive traversal along one path before exploring other options.
answers.b: DFS can be used to find the shortest path between two nodes in an unweighted graph.
answers.c: DFS can be implemented using a stack or recursion.
answers.d: DFS can be used in topological sorting.

explanations.a: Incorrect. DFS explores a path as deeply as possible before backtracking, so this describes its depth-first behavior.
explanations.b: Correct. DFS does not guarantee a shortest path in an unweighted graph; the first path it finds may not have the minimum number of edges.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Iterative DFS uses a stack, while recursive DFS uses the function call stack.
explanations.d: Incorrect. DFS can be used to produce the ordering needed for topological sorting of a directed acyclic graph.

questions.question: 8. Consider a connected graph with 6 vertices. If DFS starts from one vertex, how many vertices will be visited?

explanations.a: Incorrect. A connected graph contains paths from the starting vertex to all other vertices.
explanations.b: Incorrect. DFS is not restricted to visiting only half of the vertices.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Because the graph is connected, all vertices are reachable from the starting vertex.
explanations.d: Correct. DFS visits every vertex reachable from its starting vertex, and in a connected graph all 6 vertices are reachable.

questions.question: 9. In an undirected graph, what does a DFS tree edge represent?

answers.a: An edge that connects a newly discovered vertex to the vertex from which it was discovered.
answers.b: An edge that must connect two already visited vertices.
answers.c: An edge that is automatically removed after traversal.
answers.d: An edge that always connects vertices at the same depth.

explanations.a: Correct. A DFS tree edge records the connection through which a previously undiscovered vertex is reached during DFS.
explanations.b: Incorrect. A DFS tree edge is associated with discovering a new vertex, rather than connecting two vertices that were already discovered.
explanations.c: Incorrect. DFS does not remove edges from the original graph.
explanations.d: Incorrect. A DFS tree edge connects a vertex with its DFS parent and therefore generally connects different depths.
